transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I guess what brings me in is that ever since I stopped working, I just can’t seem to slow down. I’m up and moving from one little job around the house to the next, all day long. It's almost like I still have a crew waiting on me to get things done. I just can't seem to stop and take a break.
How has your mood been feeling overall during this time when you've been so busy with these tasks around the house?

My mood? It's fine, really. I mean, I'm not feeling down or sad or anything like that. I just... well, I just feel like I need to keep moving all the time. But overall, I feel okay. Just a normal mood, I guess, maybe a little annoyed that I can't just sit and watch a ballgame in peace, but I'm not depressed or anything.
When you stopped working, did this constant need to keep moving and stay busy start right around that time, or have you always been someone who finds it hard to sit still and relax?

Well, I suppose I've always liked being active, but... it really became a real problem after I retired. I did handyman work for a living, and I finally stopped doing that about a year and two months ago. So, yeah, right around that time is when it really started bothering me that I couldn't just sit still.
Have you noticed any changes in your memory, concentration, or ability to think clearly since you stopped working, or do you ever feel confused or disoriented?
No, my memory is fine. I don't feel confused or anything like that. I can think just as clearly as I always have. It's really just the not being able to sit still that's bothering me.
When you're going through the day feeling like you need to keep moving, do you notice any physical sensations like your heart racing, trembling, sweating, or muscle tension?

No, I haven't noticed anything like that. My heart doesn't race, and I don't get the shakes or sweat or anything. My muscles feel fine. It's really just... well, I just have this constant urge to be up and doing something, you know? But physically, no, I don't have any of those other things going on.

Since you retired, have you experienced any other significant changes in your life—like problems with your relationships, your sleep, or how you're managing financially—or is it really just this difficulty sitting still that's been the main issue?

Well, it has caused some problems, mainly with other people relying on me. I've always been pretty independent, but lately... my wife has had to take over keeping the calendar and, you know, checking behind me to make sure things actually get done. And I've had to apologize to the folks at the community center and my gardening group more than once because I just... I let them down. I'd forget I was supposed to be there or I'd show up and just wander off to do something else. So, yeah, it's definitely affecting things outside of just me feeling restless.

When you forget to show up to things like the community center or your gardening group, or when you wander off and do something else instead—do you actually remember making the commitment in the first place, or is it that you forget you made those plans?

Well, it's more like... I know I made the plans, but then the day comes and it just slips my mind entirely. Lately, I've been forgetting all sorts of day-to-day things. Like, I'll forget to return calls from the folks at the community center, or I won't remember to pay a bill until my wife reminds me. And with the garden group, I'll show up, but I'll realize I completely forgot to bring the supplies I promised I'd pick up. It just goes right out of my head.

Before you retired about a year ago, would you say your memory was noticeably better than it is now, or has your ability to remember things like appointments and tasks always been about the same as it is currently?

Well, honestly, it's always been about the same. Even way back when I was in grade school, my teachers used to tell my parents that I was bright but just... scattered. I was always losing my pencils, calling out answers without raising my hand, and they constantly had to remind me to actually finish my work before I could go out for recess. So, no, it's not a new thing since I retired. It's pretty much just how I've always been.

You mentioned being scattered since grade school, but I'm wondering—back then and through your working years, did this scattered behavior and restlessness actually cause real problems for you, or was it just something your teachers noticed but that didn't really interfere with your life?

Well, it definitely caused some problems. I mean, it wasn't just teachers noticing it. I struggled to keep up with my assignments, and I got into trouble a fair bit for being disruptive. And even when I started working, I had a hard time staying organized and keeping track of deadlines. It's always been something I've had to work around, you know? It just feels like it's gotten harder to manage now that I don't have the structure of a job.
